```{r}
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
reg <- filter(institutions, level == "4-year", !is.na(pct_pell), !is.na(grad_rate_bach_6yr), bach_cohort >= 30) |>
  mutate(half = as.integer(grad_rate_bach_6yr >= 50))
fit <- glm(half ~ pct_pell, family = binomial, data = reg)
b0 <- round(coef(fit)[1], 2)
b1 <- round(coef(fit)[2], 3)
or10 <- round(exp(10 * coef(fit)[2]), 2)
share_half <- round(100 * mean(reg$half))
p_at <- function(x) round(100 * predict(fit, data.frame(pct_pell = x), type = "response"))
crossover <- round(-coef(fit)[1] / coef(fit)[2])
lpm <- lm(half ~ pct_pell, data = reg)
lpm0 <- round(100 * predict(lpm, data.frame(pct_pell = 0)))
lpm100 <- round(100 * predict(lpm, data.frame(pct_pell = 100)))
acc <- round(100 * mean(as.integer(fitted(fit) >= 0.5) == reg$half))
```

::: {.lesson-eyebrow}
Test · Lesson 6 of 6
:::

The last lesson asked how many points of completion go with a point of Pell share. Many IR questions are not "how many" but "whether": will this student be retained, will this applicant enroll, did this institution graduate most of its cohort. The outcome is a yes or a no, and a straight line is the wrong shape for it. This lesson fits the right shape, the logistic curve, and spends most of its time on how to say what the fit means.

The example stays with `r v("pct_pell")` and the same `r fmt(nrow(reg))` four-year institutions with a bachelor's cohort of at least 30, but the outcome is now a yes or no: does the institution graduate **at least half** of its cohort within six years? `r share_half`% do. An IR office would usually fit this model one student at a time, with retention or completion as the outcome. The institution table has one row per college, so the yes or no here is about a college, and everything else carries over.

**You will be able to:** fit a logistic regression, turn a coefficient into an odds ratio and a predicted probability, explain why the straight line fails, and report the result in a sentence a dean can use.

## Watch it move {.beat data-beat="1 · Watch it move"}

Every dot is an institution: at the top if it graduates at least half its cohort, at the bottom if not. Drag the sliders to place your own curve. The score is the log-likelihood, how well the curve's probabilities agree with what happened. Then switch to maximum likelihood to see the curve no other curve can beat.

::: {.lab-anim}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
inst = FileAttachment("data/institutions.csv").csv({typed: true})
reg = inst
  .filter(d => d.level === "4-year" && d.pct_pell != null && d.grad_rate_bach_6yr != null && d.bach_cohort >= 30)
  .map(d => ({...d, half: d.grad_rate_bach_6yr >= 50 ? 1 : 0}))

logistic = (b0, b1, x) => 1 / (1 + Math.exp(-(b0 + b1 * x)))

loglik = (b0, b1) => d3.sum(reg, d => {
  const p = Math.min(1 - 1e-12, Math.max(1e-12, logistic(b0, b1, d.pct_pell)));
  return d.half ? Math.log(p) : Math.log(1 - p);
})

mle = {
  let b0 = 0, b1 = 0;
  for (let it = 0; it < 50; it++) {
    let g0 = 0, g1 = 0, h00 = 0, h01 = 0, h11 = 0;
    for (const d of reg) {
      const x = d.pct_pell, p = logistic(b0, b1, x), w = p * (1 - p);
      g0 += d.half - p; g1 += (d.half - p) * x;
      h00 += w; h01 += w * x; h11 += w * x * x;
    }
    const det = h00 * h11 - h01 * h01;
    const s0 = (h11 * g0 - h01 * g1) / det, s1 = (h00 * g1 - h01 * g0) / det;
    b0 += s0; b1 += s1;
    if (Math.abs(s0) + Math.abs(s1) < 1e-10) break;
  }
  return {b0, b1};
}

lpm = {
  const mx = d3.mean(reg, d => d.pct_pell), my = d3.mean(reg, d => d.half);
  let sxy = 0, sxx = 0;
  for (const d of reg) { sxy += (d.pct_pell - mx) * (d.half - my); sxx += (d.pct_pell - mx) ** 2; }
  const slope = sxy / sxx;
  return {slope, intercept: my - slope * mx};
}
```

```{ojs}
viewof b1 = Inputs.range([-0.2, 0.1], {label: "Slope (per Pell point)", step: 0.001, value: 0})
viewof showLine = Inputs.toggle({label: "Show the straight-line fit", value: false})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
logitNode = d3.create("svg").attr("class", "lab-svg").node()

logitPlot = {
  const width = 860, height = 420, margin = {top: 20, right: 20, bottom: 48, left: 56};
  const reduce = window.matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches;
  const dur = reduce ? 0 : 500;
  const c0 = curvemode === "Maximum likelihood" ? mle.b0 : b0;
  const c1 = curvemode === "Maximum likelihood" ? mle.b1 : b1;
  const x = d3.scaleLinear().domain([0, 100]).range([margin.left, width - margin.right]);
  const y = d3.scaleLinear().domain([-0.12, 1.12]).range([height - margin.bottom, margin.top]);
  const jitter = d3.randomNormal.source(d3.randomLcg(3))(0, 0.03);
  const jit = new Map(reg.map(d => [d.unitid, Math.max(-0.08, Math.min(0.08, jitter()))]));
  const xs = d3.range(0, 100.5, 1);
  const curve = d3.line().x(v => x(v)).y(v => y(logistic(c0, c1, v)));
  const straight = d3.line().x(v => x(v)).y(v => y(Math.max(-0.12, Math.min(1.12, lpm.intercept + lpm.slope * v))));

  const svg = d3.select(logitNode);
  svg.attr("viewBox", [0, 0, width, height]);
  const layer = name => { let g = svg.select(`g.${name}`); if (g.empty()) g = svg.append("g").attr("class", name); return g; };
  const gx = layer("axis"), gy = layer("axisy"), gd = layer("dots"), gl = layer("fitline"), gs = layer("straight"), gm = layer("mid"), glab = layer("labels");

  if (gx.selectAll("*").empty()) {
    gx.attr("transform", `translate(0,${height - margin.bottom})`).call(d3.axisBottom(x).ticks(10).tickSizeOuter(0));
    gy.attr("transform", `translate(${margin.left},0)`).call(d3.axisLeft(y).tickValues([0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1]).tickFormat(d3.format(".0%")).tickSizeOuter(0));
    glab.append("text").attr("class", "axis-label").attr("x", width - margin.right).attr("y", height - 10).attr("text-anchor", "end").text("Percent of undergraduates with Pell grants");
    glab.append("text").attr("class", "axis-label").attr("transform", `translate(14,${margin.top}) rotate(-90)`).attr("text-anchor", "end").text("Graduates at least half of the cohort");
    glab.append("text").attr("font-size", 12).attr("fill", "var(--lab-muted)").attr("x", x(1)).attr("y", y(1) - 8).text("Yes");
    glab.append("text").attr("font-size", 12).attr("fill", "var(--lab-muted)").attr("x", x(1)).attr("y", y(0) + 16).text("No");
    gd.selectAll("circle").data(reg, d => d.unitid).join("circle")
      .attr("r", 2.4).attr("fill", d => d.half ? "var(--lab-primary)" : "var(--lab-accent)").attr("fill-opacity", 0.45)
      .attr("cx", d => x(d.pct_pell)).attr("cy", d => y(d.half + jit.get(d.unitid)))
      .append("title").text(d => `${d.name}\nPell ${d.pct_pell}%, completion ${d.grad_rate_bach_6yr}%`);
    gs.append("path").attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "var(--lab-muted)").attr("stroke-width", 2).attr("stroke-dasharray", "6 4");
    gl.append("path").attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke-width", 3).attr("stroke-linecap", "round");
    gm.append("line").attr("stroke", "var(--lab-muted)").attr("stroke-width", 1).attr("stroke-dasharray", "2 3").attr("y1", y(0)).attr("y2", y(1));
    gm.append("text").attr("font-size", 11).attr("fill", "var(--lab-muted)").attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("y", y(1) - 8);
  }

  const t = svg.transition().duration(dur).ease(d3.easeCubicOut);
  gl.select("path").attr("stroke", curvemode === "Maximum likelihood" ? "var(--lab-ink)" : "var(--lab-accent)")
    .transition(t).attr("d", curve(xs));
  gs.select("path").attr("opacity", showLine ? 1 : 0).attr("d", straight(xs));

  const cross = c1 !== 0 ? -c0 / c1 : NaN;
  const showMid = Number.isFinite(cross) && cross >= 0 && cross <= 100;
  gm.attr("opacity", showMid ? 1 : 0);
  if (showMid) {
    gm.select("line").transition(t).attr("x1", x(cross)).attr("x2", x(cross));
    gm.select("text").text(`50% at Pell ${d3.format(".0f")(cross)}`).transition(t).attr("x", x(cross));
  }

  return svg.node();
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
logitReadout = {
  const isMle = curvemode === "Maximum likelihood";
  const c0 = isMle ? mle.b0 : b0, c1 = isMle ? mle.b1 : b1;
  const yours = loglik(c0, c1), best = loglik(mle.b0, mle.b1);
  const base = d3.mean(reg, d => d.half);
  const flat = loglik(Math.log(base / (1 - base)), 0);
  const p = v => d3.format(".0%")(logistic(c0, c1, v));
  return html`<div class="lab-readout">
    <div><span class="k">Intercept</span><span class="val ${isMle ? "" : "accent"}">${d3.format(".2f")(c0)}</span></div>
    <div><span class="k">Slope</span><span class="val ${isMle ? "" : "accent"}">${d3.format("+.3f")(c1)}</span></div>
    <div><span class="k">Log-likelihood</span><span class="val">${d3.format(",.1f")(yours)}</span></div>
    <div><span class="k">Best possible</span><span class="val">${d3.format(",.1f")(best)}</span></div>
    <div><span class="k">Odds ratio per 10 Pell points</span><span class="val">${d3.format(".2f")(Math.exp(10 * c1))}</span></div>
    <div><span class="k">P(yes) at Pell 20 / 40 / 60</span><span class="val">${p(20)} / ${p(40)} / ${p(60)}</span></div>
  </div>
  <p class="lab-hint">${isMle
    ? `No other curve scores higher than ${d3.format(",.1f")(best)}. A flat curve at the overall rate of ${d3.format(".0%")(base)} scores ${d3.format(",.1f")(flat)}; the gap between the two is what Pell share buys you.`
    : `Your curve is ${d3.format(",.1f")(best - yours)} below the maximum. Log-likelihoods are negative and closer to zero is better. A flat curve at the overall rate scores ${d3.format(",.1f")(flat)}.`}</p>`;
}
```

:::

Three things to try:

1. **Start flat.** Leave the slope at 0 and move the intercept. The curve is a horizontal line, and the best flat line sits at the overall rate of `r share_half`%. That is the baseline: a model that knows nothing about Pell share predicts `r share_half`% for everyone.
2. **Tilt it.** Pull the slope negative and adjust the intercept so the curve passes through the middle of the cloud, high on the left where most dots are "yes", low on the right. Watch the log-likelihood climb toward the maximum. Maximum likelihood is this search done exactly.
3. **Show the straight line.** It is the least-squares line from the last lesson fitted to 0s and 1s. It predicts `r lpm0`% at zero Pell and `r lpm100`% at 100. A probability cannot be either. The curve bends because it has to.

## Do it {.beat data-beat="2 · Do it"}

The cells below run in your browser. The model is `glm()` with `family = binomial` in R and `smf.logit()` in Python. Both report coefficients on the log-odds scale, which is why the second step in each tab is always `exp()`.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### R

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| caption: Build the yes/no outcome
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom)

inst <- read.csv("data/institutions.csv")
reg <- inst |>
  filter(level == "4-year", !is.na(pct_pell), !is.na(grad_rate_bach_6yr), bach_cohort >= 30) |>
  mutate(half = as.integer(grad_rate_bach_6yr >= 50))

reg |> count(half) |> mutate(share = round(n / sum(n), 3))
```

The fit. The slope is on the log-odds scale: each Pell point changes the log-odds of a "yes" by that amount. Nobody thinks in log-odds, so the next cell converts.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| caption: Fit the logistic regression
fit <- glm(half ~ pct_pell, family = binomial, data = reg)
tidy(fit)
```

`exp()` of a coefficient is an odds ratio: the factor the odds are multiplied by for a one-unit change in the predictor. One Pell point is a small step, so the cell also reports the ratio for ten points, which is a difference between two real institutions.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| caption: Odds ratios per point and per ten points
b <- coef(fit)[["pct_pell"]]
c(per_point = exp(b), per_10_points = exp(10 * b))
```

Odds ratios are still hard to picture. Predicted probabilities are not. `type = "response"` puts the prediction back on the probability scale.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| caption: Predicted probabilities at four Pell shares
grid <- data.frame(pct_pell = c(20, 40, 60, 80))
grid$p_half <- predict(fit, newdata = grid, type = "response")
grid
```

The picture: the dots, the logistic curve, and the straight line that would have been wrong.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| caption: Curve against straight line
ggplot(reg, aes(pct_pell, half)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.04, alpha = 0.3, color = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#8a8f96", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = binomial), se = FALSE, color = "#14213d", linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.1, 1.1)) +
  labs(
    x = "Percent of undergraduates with Pell grants", y = "Graduates at least half of the cohort",
    title = "Logistic curve (solid) and least-squares line (dashed)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

Adding a predictor works the way it did for `lm()`. With `exponentiate = TRUE`, `tidy()` reports odds ratios and their confidence intervals directly. Sector's odds ratios are relative to the first level, private for-profit.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| caption: Add control as a second predictor
fit2 <- glm(half ~ pct_pell + control, family = binomial, data = reg)
tidy(fit2, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

### Python

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| caption: Build the yes/no outcome
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

inst = pd.read_csv("data/institutions.csv")
reg = inst[(inst["level"] == "4-year") & inst["pct_pell"].notna()
           & inst["grad_rate_bach_6yr"].notna() & (inst["bach_cohort"] >= 30)].copy()
reg["half"] = (reg["grad_rate_bach_6yr"] >= 50).astype(int)

reg["half"].value_counts(normalize=True).round(3)
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| caption: Fit the logistic regression
fit = smf.logit("half ~ pct_pell", data=reg).fit(disp=0)
fit.summary2().tables[1].round(4)
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| caption: Odds ratios per point and per ten points
b = fit.params["pct_pell"]
pd.Series({"per_point": np.exp(b), "per_10_points": np.exp(10 * b)}).round(3)
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| caption: Predicted probabilities at four Pell shares
grid = pd.DataFrame({"pct_pell": [20, 40, 60, 80]})
grid["p_half"] = fit.predict(grid)
grid.round(3)
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| caption: Curve against straight line
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
xs = np.linspace(0, 100, 101)
curve = fit.predict(pd.DataFrame({"pct_pell": xs}))
line = np.polyval(np.polyfit(reg["pct_pell"], reg["half"], 1), xs)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.scatter(reg["pct_pell"], reg["half"] + rng.normal(0, 0.03, len(reg)), s=8, alpha=0.3, color="#2a78d6")
ax.plot(xs, line, color="#8a8f96", linestyle="--", label="Least-squares line")
ax.plot(xs, curve, color="#14213d", linewidth=2, label="Logistic curve")
ax.set_ylim(-0.1, 1.1)
ax.set_yticks([0, 0.5, 1], ["0%", "50%", "100%"])
ax.set_xlabel("Percent of undergraduates with Pell grants")
ax.set_ylabel("Graduates at least half of the cohort")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| caption: Add control as a second predictor
fit2 = smf.logit("half ~ pct_pell + C(control)", data=reg).fit(disp=0)
out = pd.DataFrame({"odds_ratio": np.exp(fit2.params), "p_value": fit2.pvalues})
out[["ci_low", "ci_high"]] = np.exp(fit2.conf_int())
out.round(3)
```

:::

::: {.lab-exercise data-exercise="stats2_fit"}

### Retention as the predictor

Fit a logistic regression of `half` on full-time retention, `retention_ft`, using the `reg` table. Return the **odds ratio** for one point of retention: a single number.

```{webr}
#| exercise: stats2_fit
fit_ret <- glm(half ~ ______, family = ______, data = reg)
exp(coef(fit_ret))[["retention_ft"]]
```

::: {.hint exercise="stats2_fit"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
The predictor goes on the right of the tilde. The family that makes `glm()` fit a logistic regression is `binomial`. `glm()` drops the rows where retention is missing.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="stats2_fit"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
fit_ret <- glm(half ~ retention_ft, family = binomial, data = reg)
exp(coef(fit_ret))[["retention_ft"]]
```
Each point of first-year retention multiplies the odds of graduating at least half the cohort by about 1.16. Ten points multiplies them by about 4.3. Retention is the strongest single predictor of completion in this table, which is why it is the number most early-alert programs try to move.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: stats2_fit
#| check: true
expected <- exp(coef(glm(half ~ retention_ft, family = binomial, data = reg)))[["retention_ft"]]
raw <- coef(glm(half ~ retention_ft, family = binomial, data = reg))[["retention_ft"]]
if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1 && isTRUE(abs(.result - expected) < 1e-3)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("Correct. Odds ratio %.3f per point of retention, about %.1f per ten points.", expected, expected^10))
} else if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1 && isTRUE(abs(.result - raw) < 1e-3)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the log-odds coefficient. Wrap it in exp() to get the odds ratio.")
} else if (inherits(.result, "glm")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You returned the whole model. Return the odds ratio for retention_ft as a single number.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not yet. Check the predictor name and that family = binomial.")
}
```

:::

::: {.lab-exercise data-exercise="stats2_predict"}

### Predict a probability

`fit` is the Pell model from above. Return the predicted **probability** that an institution with 40% Pell graduates at least half of its cohort. A single number between 0 and 1.

```{webr}
#| exercise: stats2_predict
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(pct_pell = 40), type = "______")
```

::: {.hint exercise="stats2_predict"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
The default prediction from a logistic `glm` is on the log-odds scale. The `type` that returns a probability is `"response"`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="stats2_predict"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(pct_pell = 40), type = "response")
```
About even odds. Forty percent Pell is close to the point where the curve crosses 50%, which is why a one-line summary of this model is "institutions above roughly 40% Pell are more likely than not to graduate under half their cohort."
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: stats2_predict
#| check: true
expected <- unname(predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(pct_pell = 40), type = "response"))
logit <- unname(predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(pct_pell = 40)))
if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1 && isTRUE(abs(.result - expected) < 1e-4)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("Correct: %.1f%%. At 40%% Pell the model is close to a coin flip.", 100 * expected))
} else if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1 && isTRUE(abs(.result - logit) < 1e-4)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the log-odds. Use type = \"response\" to get a probability.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not yet. The answer is a single number between 0 and 1.")
}
```

:::

### The same fit in Python

Fit the Pell model with `smf.logit()` and return the odds ratio for `pct_pell` as a single number.

```{pyodide}

reg["half"] = (reg["grad_rate_bach_6yr"] >= 50).astype(int)
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: stats2_py_fit
fit = smf.logit("half ~ ______", data=reg).fit(disp=0)
float(np.______(fit.params["pct_pell"]))
```

::: {.hint exercise="stats2_py_fit"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
The formula is `"half ~ pct_pell"`. The function that turns a log-odds coefficient into an odds ratio is `np.exp()`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="stats2_py_fit"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```python
fit = smf.logit("half ~ pct_pell", data=reg).fit(disp=0)
float(np.exp(fit.params["pct_pell"]))
```
:::
:::

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: stats2_py_fit
#| check: true
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
_fit = smf.logit("half ~ pct_pell", data=reg).fit(disp=0)
expected = float(np.exp(_fit.params["pct_pell"]))
raw = float(_fit.params["pct_pell"])
try:
    val = float(result)
except Exception:
    val = None
if val is not None and abs(val - expected) < 1e-3:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": f"Correct. Odds ratio {expected:.3f} per Pell point, the same as the R fit."}
elif val is not None and abs(val - raw) < 1e-3:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "That is the log-odds coefficient. Wrap it in np.exp()."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not yet. Expected a single number, the odds ratio for pct_pell."}
feedback
```

:::

## In your stack {.beat data-beat="4 · In your stack"}

Neither Excel nor DAX has a logistic regression function. Both can still hold the model, and Excel can fit it. The `logistic` sheet in [ir-lab.xlsx](data/ir-lab.xlsx) has the rows, the likelihood column, and the fitted coefficients in place.

::: {.panel-tabset group="stack"}

### Excel

`LOGEST` is not this. It fits an exponential growth curve. Logistic regression in Excel is a log-likelihood column and Solver, and the sheet lays it out so each step is visible.

| Column | Formula in row 2 |
|---|---|
| Outcome `half` | `=IF(E2>=50,1,0)` |
| Probability | `=1/(1+EXP(-($K$4+$K$5*D2)))` |
| Log-likelihood | `=F2*LN(G2)+(1-F2)*LN(1-G2)` |
| Total | `=SUM(H2:H1649)` |

Then Data, Solver: set the total cell to Max by changing the intercept and slope cells, with the GRG Nonlinear method. Starting from 0 and 0 it reaches the coefficients in the R tab. If Solver is missing, enable it under File, Options, Add-ins.

Once the coefficients are in cells, everything else is arithmetic:

- **Odds ratio** per point: `=EXP($K$5)`. Per ten points: `=EXP(10*$K$5)`.
- **Probability at a given Pell share** in cell K10: `=1/(1+EXP(-($K$4+$K$5*K10)))`.
- **Crossover**, the Pell share where the curve hits 50%: `=-$K$4/$K$5`.

The `Regression` tool in Data Analysis will happily fit a straight line to the 0/1 column. That is the dashed line from the animation, and its predictions leave the 0 to 1 range at both ends.

### Power BI

::: {.ir-powerbi data-powerbi-page="regression" data-powerbi-title="Pell and completion"}
**Interactive report: not connected yet.** Download the [Power BI project](data/ir-lab-powerbi.zip) to explore this lesson in Power BI Desktop. The embedded report will appear here once it is connected.
:::

DAX cannot fit a logistic regression. `LINESTX` is linear only, and there is no likelihood maximizer. The workable pattern is to fit the model in R or Python, put the coefficients in a two-row table, and let DAX do the scoring. Enter the table by hand with Enter Data:

```
term        estimate
Intercept    3.002
pct_pell    -0.0735
```

Then two measures give you the predicted probability for any selection, and a what-if parameter turns it into the slider from the animation:

```dax
Logit Intercept = CALCULATE ( MAX ( coefficients[estimate] ), coefficients[term] = "Intercept" )
Logit Pell Slope = CALCULATE ( MAX ( coefficients[estimate] ), coefficients[term] = "pct_pell" )

Predicted P(half) =
VAR pell = SELECTEDVALUE ( institutions[pct_pell], [Pell What If Value] )
RETURN 1 / ( 1 + EXP ( - ( [Logit Intercept] + [Logit Pell Slope] * pell ) ) )

Odds Ratio per 10 Pell Points = EXP ( 10 * [Logit Pell Slope] )
```

A calculated column with the same arithmetic scores every institution, and a matrix of predicted against actual `half` is the confusion table from the animation's readout:

```dax
Predicted Half =
VAR p = 1 / ( 1 + EXP ( - ( 3.002 - 0.0735 * institutions[pct_pell] ) ) )
RETURN IF ( ISBLANK ( institutions[pct_pell] ), BLANK (), IF ( p >= 0.5, 1, 0 ) )
```

Two built-in visuals do related work without code. The **Key influencers** visual takes a yes/no field as the target and reports which values of other fields raise its likelihood, which is a logistic-style analysis with the odds already translated into "x times more likely". And the **Python visual** or **R visual** runs the `Do it` code inside the report, at the cost of needing a Python or R installation on every machine that refreshes it.

:::

## Before you leave

::: {.takeaways}
1. **A yes or no needs a curve.** The straight line predicts probabilities below 0 and above 1. Logistic regression bends so it cannot.
2. **Coefficients are log-odds. Report odds ratios or probabilities.** "Ten more Pell points cuts the odds of majority completion by about half" is a sentence. "The coefficient is `r b1`" is not.
3. **Probabilities beat odds ratios for most readers.** Pick two or three realistic values of the predictor and report the predicted probability at each: `r p_at(20)`% at 20% Pell, `r p_at(40)`% at 40, `r p_at(60)`% at 60.
4. **Same caveat as the line.** This is an association across institutions in one year. It is not the effect of Pell on any campus, and the sector model shows part of it is sector.
:::

This is the last lesson in the Test track. The Model track picks up where it leaves off: **Split before you fit** turns predicted probabilities into a classifier and asks how well it does on institutions it has never seen.
